newsitem.title: FRANCE: French government rebuffs call for Algeria action.
newsitem.headline: French government rebuffs call for Algeria action.

text.p: The French government rebuffed calls for a political initiative on Algeria on Monday after opposition leader Lionel Jospin tried to shake the establishment out of silence on bloodshed in the former North African colony.

"Algeria is an independent country and for the moment we think it is the responsiblity of the Algerian people, Algerian leaders, to find solutions to their own problems," Foreign Minister Herve de Charette said on a visit to Denmark.
Jospin faced reluctance in his own Socialist Party as well as from the centre-right government to taking a higher profile.

Algerian President Liamine Zeroual on Friday blamed a surge of violence by Moslem fundamentalist guerrillas since the start of the Moslem fasting month of Ramadan on a foreign conspiracy and vowed to exterminate what he called "terrorists".

His government threatened action against the independent Algerian press after newspapers criticised the absence of any political solution in his televised address. Algerian security forces on Sunday prevented a rally by opposition politicians to demand dialogue with outlawed Islamists and an end to bloodshed.

"The Algerian government will overcome terrorism, modernise the country and return some hope to the population only if it accepts some change and particularly dialogue with democratic forces," Jospin said in an interview with the daily Liberation.
He urged France to consult its European Union partners on a joint initiative, saying no one dared discuss Algeria as long as Paris did not move.

Jospin received help from centre-right ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing, who said he would chair a special session of the parliamentary foreign affairs committee to question the government on its analysis of the situation in Algeria.

"Given the multiplication of bloody attacks in Algeria", the former president said, he had decided to ask the government "what attitude France and the EU should take to contribute to the search for a democratic, peaceful solution".
But former Socialist prime minister Michel Rocard said there was little that France or Europe could do, and urged caution in the light of Paris's colonial background.
Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux denied that France had been silent on the latest violence, which has taken at least 250 lives in the last two weeks.

"France firmly condemns terrorism and violence from whatever source. Algeria is a sovereign state...A democratic process has been put in place. Liamine Zeroual was elected in conditions judged legitimate and satisfactory by the international community," he told a daily briefing.

The French authorities have taken the lowest possible public profile on Algeria since a wave of bombings in France in 1995 by Moslem militants bent on punishing Paris for its perceived support for the military-dominated Algiers government.

Zeroual cancelled a planned meeting with Jacques Chirac at the United Nations in 1995 after the French leader suggested financial aid should be tied to democratic reforms. Algerian officials accused France of neo-colonial interference.

Paris has delayed the opening of new talks on financial aid after a previous six billion franc ($1.1 billion) credit line expired. But experts say Algeria, its revenues boosted by rising world oil and gas prices and a new trans-Mediterranean gas pipeline to Spain, is not short of cash.
Government officials argue privately that France can do little to bring about an improvement in Algeria and that any French initiative would be counter-productive.
Intellectuals, who challenged the political establishment on the conflict in former Yugoslavia, have been strangely silent on Algeria, saying they find both sides equally repulsive.

The secular French media have no sympathy for the Moslem insurgents who launched a brutal civil war after the army intervened in 1992 to cancel a general election which the Islamic Salvation Front (FIS) had been poised to win.
An estimated 60,000 people have been killed and the Algerian government has set up citizens' militias in many towns and villages to fight the guerrillas, increasing the bloodshed.
